analysis.one_liner: Bans selling or sharing personal data without consent and lets people sue violators.
analysis.headline: The Personal Data Privacy Act of 1999 never got a committee vote and died in the House Government Reform Committee at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal, state, and local agencies and all private businesses from selling or handing over a person's personal information — including Social Security numbers, medical records, driver's license numbers, school records, and credit card data — without that person's express consent, with narrow exceptions for national security, law enforcement, and regulatory purposes. It also required these agencies and companies to give people access to their own data within five business days of a request and to send an annual report of what data had been collected. People could sue in federal court if their data was misused.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal information is collected and traded by companies and government agencies — nearly everyone. Consumers could demand to see what data was held about them, get yearly reports on what was collected, and sue if their data was sold or shared without their permission.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose personal data is collected

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal, state, or local agency or private business from transferring, selling, or disclosing a person's personal data without that person's express consent, except for national security, law enforcement, or industry regulation purposes.
Gives individuals the right to see their own personal data within five business days of asking, and an annual report on what data was collected about them in the past year.
Defines personal data broadly to include Social Security numbers, medical records, driver's license and passport numbers, school records, credit card account information, and email addresses.
Creates a private right of action so individuals can sue in federal court when agencies or companies violate the law.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that buy and sell consumer data — data brokers, credit bureaus, marketers, and others — would lose the ability to trade personal information without consent and would bear compliance costs for access and annual reporting. Government agencies would face new paperwork burdens and potential lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and companies that trade data

drawbacks.text: The exceptions for national security, law enforcement, and 'regulation of an industry' are broad enough that government agencies could still share personal data widely under those headings.
Requiring an annual data report to every individual and five-business-day access responses would impose significant compliance costs on nearly every business and agency that holds personal data.
The bill was never amended or refined in committee, so questions about how it would interact with existing financial and health privacy laws were never worked through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give Americans real control over their own information — the right to say no to its sale, see what is held about them, and sue violators. The compliance costs on business and government are real but modest compared with the value of the privacy being protected, and the law-enforcement and national-security exceptions soften the burden on agencies. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Government Reform Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee a week later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on July 29, 1999, with two original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Government Reform the same day, and on August 4, 1999, referred to the Subcommittee on Civil Service.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that buy, sell, and trade consumer personal data, and agencies that share personal information, kept doing so without needing consent. Consumers remained without a federal right to see, correct, or block the sale of their own data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and agencies that trade data

for.name: Rep. Maurice D. Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Personal Data Privacy Act of 1999 on July 29, 1999.

for.name: Reps. Gerald Kleczka and George Miller
for.role: Original cosponsors, U.S. House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition — the bill died in committee without a vote, so no member ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.industry: Data brokers and consumer data marketers
industries.note: Would be barred from selling or transferring personal data without consent and would face lawsuits from consumers. Their business model depends on trading personal information the public never agreed to sell.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and financial data providers
industries.note: Would face new restrictions and compliance duties on sharing account and credit card data, though the bill predates modern data-broker rules. Consumers gain the right to access their own credit data.
Would be covered as private entities barred from disclosing email addresses and internet-identifiable data without consent. Would gain clearer rules but lose a source of sellable data.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local government agencies
industries.note: Would face restrictions on sharing personal data and new duties to provide access and annual reports, though broad exceptions for law enforcement, national security, and regulation would preserve most existing government data-sharing.
